source.title: Scaling Laws for Agent Harnesses via Effective Feedback Compute
source.authors: Xuan-Liang Zhang; Dingzirui Wang; Keyan Xu; Qing-Fu Zhu; Wan-Xiang Che

page_placements.theme: Sampling, ensembles, search and interaction provide conditional scaling gains

record.file_problem: The provided text includes the paper body and appendices through the final supplied figure captions; no garbling or truncation is evident.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses a power-law failure-rate model to analyze agent-harness performance, but does not test pretraining loss against parameter count, training tokens, or training compute, nor the other listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study measures agent-task failure or success against effective-feedback coordinates and reports harness interventions. Those are adjacent to, but not measurements of, the listed pretraining-loss and model-scaling versions. Rows below record the distinct agent-harness scaling results as findings outside the listed versions. The references to Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. are background, not results from those studies.
record.test_reason: The study fits a power-law failure model E(z)=E∞+Az^−α to agent-harness task failure rates against test-time quantities (tokens, tool calls, EFC) for fixed API models. It does not measure pretraining loss, vary parameters, training tokens or training compute, or relate downstream performance to model scale or pretraining loss. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only as background in related work. It borrows the power-law form as a tool for a different construct (inference-time agent scaling), so no listed version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as paraphrased. The authors conclude that harness scaling is better explained by durable, task-sufficient effective feedback than by raw test-time expenditure, and that EFC-Adapter improves the accuracy–cost tradeoff. They make no claims about pretraining scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits failure-rate power laws for agent-task outcomes against EFC and related predictors, rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss against model parameters, training tokens, or training compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported harness-efficiency rankings vary by benchmark slice: HumanEval favors H5/H6, Terminal-Bench has low efficiency across harnesses, and SWE-bench favors H0/H3 over H5/H6. Task-demand normalization also depends on calibrated task distribution and fitted demand factors.

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic tasks, a power-law failure model fits task-demand-normalized Oracle-EFC with R² = 0.99. Raw tokens give R² = 0.27 and other raw-compute predictors give R² ≤ 0.16.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Agent-harness failure rates follow a power law in task-normalized effective feedback much better than in raw test-time expenditure.

fits_no_version.finding: With raw budgets matched, higher feedback quality raises success from 0.27 to 0.90.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feedback quality, not raw inference budget, drives agent success at fixed budget.

fits_no_version.finding: EFC-based coordinates predict failure on held-out, real and prospective traces (R² 0.82–0.95), while raw expenditure gives negative R² on real traces. EFC-Adapter raises pass rate (61.2% to 68.2%) and cuts realized cost (213.8 to 85.1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Trace-derived effective-feedback measures predict agent-task outcomes out of sample, and EFC-aware control improves the accuracy–cost tradeoff.

record.problems: The results concern selected synthetic tasks and automatically verifiable agent benchmarks, not language-model pretraining loss or parameter/data/compute scaling. Run and task counts are not stated in the supplied text. Many figures show uncertainty intervals without giving their numeric bounds; most main-text aggregate fit values have no uncertainty reported.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix E.3 model-specific repetitions and figure-level predictor comparisons are not separately extracted; they repeat the adjacent EFC-versus-agent-outcome analyses and do not test any listed claim version.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute: not measured.
Extrapolation from small to large pretraining runs: not measured.
Architecture shape effects at fixed parameter count: not measured.
Other modalities or training regimes (repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer): not measured. Inference-time agent-harness fits are a different construct.
Downstream performance versus model scale or pretraining loss: not measured. The three API models are not ordered by scale, and no scale analysis is given.
Fit-dependence of pretraining exponents or compute-optimal splits: not measured.

record.verdict_notes: The 'scaling law' here is an inference-time agent-harness fit with median-normalized predictors over three fixed API models, with no variation in model scale. Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. appear only in related work. The R² values are fits of the authors' own coordinate. Run and task counts are not stated.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, training tokens, and training compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small pretraining runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation for a fixed training-compute budget.
Effects of architecture depth, width, and other details on pretraining loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream performance as a function of model scale or pretraining loss.
Setup-dependent pretraining scaling exponents, compute-optimal splits, or departures from single power laws.
